text: Cooking and eating quality of milled rice is described in the source through three related chemical traits. Gelatinization temperature (សីតុណ្ហភាពដែលធ្វើឲ្យអង្ករឆ្អិន) is the temperature at which starch in the grain absorbs water and swells irreversibly during cooking; rice with a lower gelatinization temperature generally cooks faster and holds together less firmly, while rice with a higher gelatinization temperature takes longer to cook through. Gel consistency (ស្ថេរភាពនៃការវិលបានក្រោយឆ្អិន) describes how firm or soft cooked rice becomes after it cools — a hard/firm gel consistency corresponds to cooked rice that stays firmer and separates more, while a soft gel consistency corresponds to softer, stickier cooked rice. Amylose content (អត្រាអាមីឡូស) is the share of one particular starch type in the grain, generally grouped by the source as low (roughly under 20%), intermediate (roughly 20-25%), and high (above roughly 25%) — though the exact cutoffs used vary by classification system. Higher-amylose rice tends to cook up drier, firmer, and separates more (typical of many everyday cooking varieties), while low-amylose rice — including many Japonica-type and glutinous varieties — cooks up softer and stickier. Together these three traits largely explain why different varieties are preferred for different uses: rice destined for everyday cooking is often bred and selected for an intermediate amylose range that balances separateness with softness, while specialty or glutinous rice intentionally has low amylose for a sticky texture. The source notes that processors and buyers assess these traits with simple lab tests — an alkali spreading test for gelatinization temperature, an amylose test, and a gel consistency test — which require basic laboratory equipment rather than being something a farmer can check by eye in the field, but understanding what these terms mean can help farmers and traders communicate with millers or buyers who specify a particular eating-quality profile. (Note: the percentage cutoffs and measurement ranges given here for amylose content and gel consistency are illustrative figures from the source's reference tables, not universal fixed standards.)
